Doorkeeper (Minor Order)
DOR-kee-per
n. (the porter or ostiarius, the first of the Western minor orders; he kept the church doors, rang the bells and opened the book for the preacher)
Latin ostiarius, from ostium, a door; the English porter is from porta, a gate, and renders the same office.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The ostiarius or porter was the lowest of the minor orders, and at his ordination the bishop handed him the keys of the church with the charge to open the house of God to the faithful and close it against the unworthy, to ring the bells, and to open the book for the preacher. The office is the only one of the four with a clear Old Testament ancestry, for the temple had porters in large numbers, ordained by David and Samuel: “All these which were chosen to be porters in the gates were two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office” (1Ch 9:22). The office also has the most famous line in the Psalter attached to it, said by a man kept outside: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10). The comparison is between the meanest place inside and the best place outside.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines doorkeeper as a porter, one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment; and threshold as the door-sill, the entrance or gate of a house.

expand to see more

DOORKEEPER, n. A porter; one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment.

PORTER, n. A man that has the charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper.

THRESHOLD, n. The door-sill; the plank, stone or piece of timber which lies at the bottom or under a door, particularly of a dwelling house, church, temple or the like.

COURT, n. In Scripture, an enclosed space or yard belonging to the tabernacle or temple.

TABERNACLE, n. A tent. A temporary habitation. Among the Israelites, a movable building, so contrived as to be taken to pieces with ease and reconstructed.

Key Scripture

1Ch 9:22 — "All these which were chosen to be porters in the gates were two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office."

Psa 84:10 — "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."

Psa 84:2 — "My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God."

Psa 84:11 — "For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly."

Modern Corruption

The porter with the church keys, the one minor order with a temple ancestry, and the psalm of a man outside the door.

expand to see more

The corruption is the doorkeeper who forgets which side of the door he is guarding — the office of admitting and excluding, exercised for reasons the Scripture does not supply. A church door closed against the poor, the unfashionable or the inconvenient is being kept by a porter who has substituted his own list for his bishop's. The psalm's whole force depends on the house being open to someone who longs for it: “My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD” (Psa 84:2).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalm's arithmetic, which values the lowest position in God's house above the best elsewhere, and the promise that follows it: “no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly” (Psa 84:11). A man content to keep a door in that house has understood something about the house. The office is low and the location is everything.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin ostiarius, a doorkeeper; Hebrew shoer (H7778), a porter or gatekeeper; Hebrew saph (H5592), a threshold; Hebrew chatser (H2691), a court; Hebrew kasaph (H3700), to long for.

expand to see more

Latin ostiarius — from ostium, a door; the porter of the minor orders.

Hebrew shoer (H7778) — a gatekeeper, a porter; “chosen to be porters in the gates” (1Ch 9:22).

Hebrew saph (H5592) — a threshold, a doorway; the word behind doorkeeper in the psalm.

Hebrew chatser (H2691) — a court, an enclosure; “fainteth for the courts of the LORD” (Psa 84:2).

Hebrew tamim (H8549) — upright, complete; “them that walk uprightly” (Psa 84:11).

Usage

"“than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10) — the whole comparison."

"“did ordain in their set office” (1Ch 9:22) — porters ordained by a king and a prophet."

"“no good thing will he withhold” (Psa 84:11) — the promise to the man at the door."
